title: Learnable latent embeddings for joint behavioural and neural analysis | Nature
summary: Mapping behavioural actions to neural activity is a fundamental goal of neuroscience. As our ability to record large neural and behavioural data increases, there is growing interest in modelling neural dynamics during adaptive behaviours to probe neural representations1–3. In particular, although neural latent embeddings can reveal underlying correlates of behaviour, we lack nonlinear techniques that can explicitly and flexibly leverage joint behaviour and neural data to uncover neural dynamics3–5. Here, we fill this gap with a new encoding method, CEBRA, that jointly uses behavioural and neural data in a (supervised) hypothesis- or (self-supervised) discovery-driven manner to produce both consistent and high-performance latent spaces. We show that consistency can be used as a metric for uncovering meaningful differences, and the inferred latents can be used for decoding. We validate its accuracy and demonstrate our tool’s utility for both calcium and electrophysiology datasets, across sensory and motor tasks and in simple or complex behaviours across species. It allows leverage of single- and multi-session datasets for hypothesis testing or can be used label free. Lastly, we show that CEBRA can be used for the mapping of space, uncovering complex kinematic features, for the production of consistent latent spaces across two-photon and Neuropixels data, and can provide rapid, high-accuracy decoding of natural videos from visual cortex. title: Snappy
summary: 🐊 Snappy's unique approach unifies vision-language late interaction with structured OCR for region-level knowledge retrieval. Like the project? Drop a star! ⭐ Snappy implements region-level document retrieval by unifying vision-language models with OCR through spatial coordinate mapping. Unlike traditional systems that return entire pages VLMs or lack semantic grounding OCR-only, Snappy uses ColPali's patch-level similarity scores as spatial relevance filters over OCR-extracted regions operating entirely at inference time without additional training. Vision-language models like ColPali achieve state-of-the-art document retrieval by embedding pages as images with fine-grained patch representations. However, they return entire pages as retrieval units, introducing irrelevant content into RAG context windows. Conversely, OCR systems extract structured text with bounding boxes but cannot assess which regions are relevant to a query.

summary: [1/12] Instruction fine-tuned (IFT) LLMs are powerful, but how can we automatically evaluate the quality of their responses ? And what insights into IFT model specialization does this evaluation unlock ? A thread 🧵on our @emnlpmeeting 2023 paper: (1/N) ──────── [2/12] Evaluating IFT models designed to respond to arbitrary instructions, requires using eval metrics that can coherently score across vastly different tasks on an absolute scale, and that are not biased by the task's nature, nor the format of the reference answer (3/N) ──────── [3/12] Generative models used to serve a single purpose (translation, summarization), and evaluation metrics based on proximity with a gold reference (ROUGE, BLEU, F1, BertScore) correlated well with human judgement. ⚖️✅ The multi-task nature of IFT models changes that... ⚖️❌ (2/N) ──────── [4/12] To illustrate, it makes no sense here to use ROUGE to evaluate performance on open-ended creative writing tasks - a model answer that is very different from a correct "gold" reference is NOT NECESSARILY a bad answer ! (4/N) 📷 ──────── [5/12] What solutions do we have? Use more complex ref-based metrics (SBert, BertScore) ? ➡️ Same problem ❌ Implement custom scoring heuristics for every possible task? ➡️ Not scalable, and scores won't be comparable between tasks ❌ Score performance using other LLMs? ➡️ 💡 (5/N) ──────── [6/12] ⏭️We now have a good IFT model scorer, what can we do with it ? 🤔 Let's use this powerful tool to analyze how IFT models can be specialized for specific tasks and use cases (useful in industrial settings) ! 🏭 (7/N) ──────── [7/12] We show that using GPT4 to score the performance of other IFT LLMs is actually a viable option, leading to: 1⃣ Great correlation with human scores (CIT, SUM) 2⃣ Coherent scoring across tasks (CAT) 3⃣ Improved robustness w.r.t. the reference answer (TFA) Great ! 🎉 (6/N) 📷 ──────── [8/12] Through GPT4 eval, we show specializing IFT models on a given task by adding N target task samples to the training mix is done in 2 phases: 1⃣ models learn the response format, underlying task performance is stable (N < ~100) 2⃣ models improve on the task itself (N > 200) (8/N) 📷 ──────── [9/12] This means the first ~100 target task samples are "wasted" to teach the model to format its responses correctly, right ? 😨 Kind of... But turns out we can use "fake" (synthetic or randomly labeled) samples to teach format, and keep high-quality samples for phase 2 ! 📈 (9/N) ──────── [10/12] We also show that in order to finetune a LLM on a given target task with little data, it helps to start off from an Instruction Fine-Tuned model rather than a base model (up to ~200 samples) ! (10/N) 📷 ──────── [11/12] All in all, leveraging synthetic data can greatly improve data-efficiency when training a model with little data ressources ! ⚠️These findings are only made possible by using an evaluation metric (GPT4) robust to formatting biases (TFA) introduced during specialization ! (11/N) ──────── [12/12] More details, experiments and limitations are given in the paper ! 📜 Work done with great co-authors @PierreColombo6 @GautierViaud @CelineHudelot (12/N; N=12)

title: Manuel Faysse (@ManuelFaysse) — thread (23 tweets)
summary: [1/23] "What would you change in a V2 of CroissantLLM 🥐?" is a question that often pops up after talks ! While we're happy about how it turned out, and most design decisions were driven by research objectives, here's a 🧵about what we might have changed given today's knowledge ! (1/n) ──────── [2/23] CroissantLLM 🥐 is a completely open, strong 1.3B language model trained on 3T tokens with French and English in equal parts, as well as code data and translations. Along with the model, we released a benchmark for French LLMs, new data and codebases ! ──────── [3/23] 1. Tokenizer We optimized our 32k vocab tokenizer for English and French obtaining good fertilities on both languages. Recently, Gemma and LLama3 increased vocab sizes to improve multilingual coverage which makes a lot of sense in their case ! (3/n) ──────── [4/23] Better fertility means more data per training step and faster inference which compensates for larger model sizes ! In our case with a small model, a bigger vocab would have been too much of a parameter overhead so 32k was probably the best ! ✅ (4/n) ──────── [5/23] However, I would have preferred spending more time handcrafting a few tokens (numbers up to 100, punctuation patterns) and verifying the constructed vocabulary for "semantical" coherence to optimize the pre-tokenization heuristics, esp. for downstream use cases. (5/n) ──────── [6/23] 2. The scheduler 🥐 uses a classic Cosine scheduler for 3T tokens. At the time, we largely hesitated for an infinite learning rate setup as seen in the Scaling VIT paper by @giffmana. Wasn't common in NLP yet and we were too GPU poor to take risks... (6/n) ──────── [7/23] Tables have turned ! Since MiniCPM, it now seems well understood that constant lr, followed by an "annealing" phase at the very end matches cosine schedulers, and surpasses it if the annealing data mix is of higher quality ! (7/n) ──────── [8/23] 3. The data More than anything else, these last few months have taught us that data is key ! In 🥐, we took special care of collecting domain specific French data and using nicely filtered/curated internet data but it seems this could be pushed a lot further. (9/n) ──────── [9/23] Moreover, by doing so, you keep the lr high for 95% of the compute, and can test out many things quickly/cheaply for the annealing in the last 5%: synthetic data, upsampled quality sources, instructions... High iteration rates unlock many things ! 🔑 (8/n) ──────── [10/23] 2 observations: - It's becoming understood that reasoning skills are notably induced by math and coding heavy data mixes. - People (LMsys arena) and benchmarks (MMLU) seem to love models with high levels of factual knowledge. (10/n) ──────── [11/23] ... even with smaller data teams, it is possible to upsample datasets such as Wiki, OpenWebMath, high quality code data, instructions, especially during annealing for boosted performance which is what @kylelostat and co. did for the boosted Olmo 1.7 ! ──────── [12/23] We can optimize for this by largely augmenting the ratios of STEM, knowledge and reasoning datasets w.r.t. random web data like is done in Llama3 and what @YiTayML does with Reka. Obv. this is very hard to do right and often requires DoReMi /scaling laws but ... (11/n) ──────── [13/23] Ofc data work in general is as quintessential as it is hard, and simply relying on recent open high quality internet data mixes such as FineWeb by @gui_penedo or even Phi-style synthetic data from @LoubnaBenAllal1 could largely boost performance ! (13/n) ──────── [14/23] In terms of data/param ratio, it was one of the goal of 🥐 to train far longer than what should even be mildly useful according to Chinchilla laws. We were very happy to continue seeing clear log-linear improvements throughout training ! LLama3 7B draws similar conclusions ! ✅ 📷 ──────── [15/23] Recently, @antonschafer argues in that 90/10 ratios actually help the less represented language ! From CroissantLLM, my intuition was actually pretty aligned ! ──────── [16/23] Also interesting is the language ratio. In CroissantLLM, we went for a 50/50 mix between English and French to see what it would really change when compared to a 90+% English training mix ! (15/n) ──────── [17/23] While we found having tons of French boosts factual knowledge about French culture/history, I would argue from TinyLlama comparisons that French can be learnt with way less, and sampling from better quality English data would actually benefit reasoning/downstream tasks/etc. ──────── [18/23] 4. Other ideas Prefix LM training: The LLM2Vec paper shows Mistral might have also been trained with a partially non-causal attention mask. This makes sense for instruction models but also helps if we want to transform decoders as embedding or classification models ! ──────── [19/23] No regrets here: trying 50/50 was the whole point of our work ! 🧪 Where seeing lots of French and parallel data helps though is translation capabilities ! CroissantLLM truly is an amazing translation model for its size and this is another thing we got right ✅ (18/n) ──────── [20/23] 5. The model name: CroissantLLM Probably one of the best thing about the model, thanks @psanfernandes ! 🚀 People keep offering us croissants since the release which is an awesome side effect ! (21/n) ──────── [21/23] This is something @Muennighoff also does in GritLM a posteriori, having such an objective during pretraining might go a long way in blurring the boundaries between encoders and decoders and I would love to try ! (20/n) ──────── [22/23] I'm gonna stop here, thread is already too long ! tl;dr is that it's a fast moving field and there's lots of tricks still to be discovered ! Super excited for what's next ! 🥐 (22/22) ──────── [23/23] CroissantLLM 🥐 report is here for those interested: Work started last August with (amongst others) @PierreColombo6 @nunonmg @psanfernandes who all got nice continued pretraining experience since (and perhaps divergent opinions) !

title: Manuel Faysse (@ManuelFaysse) — thread (12 tweets)
summary: [1/12] 🚨 Introducing "ColPali: Efficient Document Retrieval with Vision Language Models" ! We use Vision LLMs + late interaction to improve document retrieval (RAG, search engines, etc.), solely using the image representation of document pages ! 🧵(1/N) ──────── [2/12] Currently, to perform document retrieval (ie. for RAG), complex pipelines exist, that may include OCR, layout detection and segmentation, figure captioning, chunking, then using text embedding models to index document passages in a vector database for future retrieval ... (2/N) ──────── [3/12] This indexing process can be slow, propagates errors, and struggles to consider the more visual elements of a page (tables, figures, images but also fonts, etc...) Our concept ? Just embed the page image directly ! (3/N) 📷 ──────── [4/12] In practice, we use PaliGemma (SigLip vision encoder + Gemma 2B text model trained on joint vision language tasks) to create multiple high quality, contextualized embeddings of image patches in text space to create a multi-vector document representation. (4/N) ──────── [5/12] At runtime, we leverage ColBERT-style @lateinteraction mechanisms to efficiently match query tokens to document patches ! We call the model ColPali ! (5/N) 📷 ──────── [6/12] We introduce ViDoRe, the Visual Document Retrieval Benchmark, to assess retrievers on their capacity to retrieve visually rich information in docs, with tasks spanning various topics, modalities (figures, tables, text), and languages ! (6/N) ──────── [7/12] ColPali outperforms all other evaluated systems, including baselines with Claude Sonnet used to caption all visual elements ! Beyond performance, ColPali enables orders of magnitude faster indexing ! Tons of ablations in the paper ! (7/N) 📷 ──────── [8/12] ViDoRe is linked to a HF leaderboard and we hope to see many models trying out this new "Retrieving in Vision Space" paradigm ! (8/N) ──────── [9/12] Tons more in the paper ! All resources are in the HF organization and will keep on coming! Joint work with amazing coauthors @sibille_hugues @tonywu_71 @PierreColombo6 amongst others ! (10/N) ──────── [10/12] Other interesting finding, our technique enables us to visualize which patches of a document stand out w.r.t. a given query. Here the term <hour> matches patches containing words like "hourly" but also the x-axis representing time, showcasing good chart comprehension ! The MTEB benchmark is sadly dead, and doesn't provide a good signal anymore. It is mostly: Who overfits the hardest.

title: Manuel Faysse (@ManuelFaysse)
summary:
🧵 Stella Embeddings: What's the big deal? (a mini explanation thread)
If you enjoy RAG Twitter, or compulsively check the MTEB leaderboard, you might've come across the "Stella" (and now, Jasper) models.
They seem suspiciously good, even though you've never heard of them before. Well, let's begin with a spoiler: they're good, period.
✨ Stella is really cool, for a few reasons:
- It's a piece of independent research into topics that aren't the current mainstream way of doing things, with fantastic results to back it up
- It's specifically designed to avoid overfitting and maximize generalization
🏆 Let's take a step back to understand a big piece of signal that makes the Stella embeddings special: MTEB
MTEB is the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark. It's a set of curated datasets designed to evaluate embedding models' capabilities on various tasks, including a mix of retrieval tasks. It's essentially the go-to when you're trying to figure out what embedding model you should try.
🤔 If you occasionally glance at the IR people Twitter discussions, you'll see that MTEB is a pretty disputed hot topic. That's because there are a lot of different setups co-existing on a single leaderboard:
- Some models attempt to be truly zero-shot (MTEB was designed as a zero-shot eval, but has a sizeable trainset)
- Some models train on some subsets/all of it, in various ways.
⚠️ Don't get me wrong: training on the training set is good, actually. It's valuable signal towards the potential of a model when finetuned on domain-appropriate data. There's absolutely nothing wrong with overfitting MTEB, in a vacuum.
The problem is that they're all blended together on the same leaderboard: it's impossible to tell who's doing what, and what level of contamination you should expect for each model. Is this model lagging behind because it's worse? Or because it's fully zero-shot? Nobody knows.
🔍 Now then, let's look at how embedding models are usually trained:
The current dominant way of training retrieval models is via the use of a contrastive loss, with little-to-no knowledge distillation (except some, such as ColBERT and ColBERTv2, or RocketQA, but it's very rarely used by MTEB mainstays).
The contrastive process uses Query <-> Document relationships, with a two-step approach:
1️⃣ First, use a lot of distantly supervised data to align the model's embedding space onto the concept of "similarity" between documents and queries. This'll be stuff like a Reddit title and its comments, Title <-> Abstract pairs from SemanticScholars, etc.
2️⃣ Then, fine-tune on higher quality annotated data, either extracted from a search engine based on which documents users clicked on after their search. Or, more generally, any dataset where human annotators labeled that the document is an answer to the query.
💭 In my opinion (and I backed it up with answerai-colbert-small!) distillation should have a bigger place. This is especially true nowadays that we have LLM-based embedders, which can be very good, but also very, very impractical given their size.
✨ And you know what? This is where Stella enters the arena!
Stella's approach takes distillation even further than previous methods: what if we only use unsupervised distillation? Why don't we get rid of those expensive, pesky labels, and complicated hard negative mining pipelines? (spoilers: this is a good idea):
🔮 Essentially, Stella takes a few really good 7B LLM-based embedding models and comes up with a multi-step learning process, involving freezing/unfreezing, dimension manipulation tricks, and much more: read the paper to find out!
📐 The main aim of this training is to work within the embedding space, seeking to minimize the geometric distances (both cosine and angular distance) between the teachers' vectors and the student model (Stella)'s outputs.
🤖 The resulting model is one that has never itself been trained on predicting query <-> document relationships like a normal retrieval model would, but instead has learned to mimic how models much smarter than itself would represent both queries and documents.
🎯 In practice, Stella models generalize amazingly well because of this. Most other small models overfit on MTEB in some ways, consciously or not: either by training on its data or, in the case of some models, by iterating on the synthetic data mix they use and selecting the one that has the best MTEB dev score.
This generally makes it kinda hard to know what's the best model for downstream use: is the model really good at generalization (what 99% of people want for their own use cases) or is the model really well fitted to MTEB? (As discussed above, this is useful signal in itself, but a lot of people want to use off-the-shelf embeddings and that's it, in which case, this is not an appropriate signal)
💫 Stella doesn't really have that problem: it's good at MTEB because it's good at generating representations that look like its teacher models' representations, and its teacher models' representations are good because they are gigantic models that are at least 7x, oftentimes 20-30x, bigger than common retrieval models.
Stella isn't trained on MTEB; at worst, it's picked up some of what its teachers knew about it. But thankfully, the teachers selected weren't overfitted on MTEB.
🎉 This means that the signal you get from Stella doing well on MTEB is that much more meaningful: you know for a fact it's good at generalizing, and so intuitively, it's a good starting point for your task.
(This has been anecdotally verified quite a few times -- on the new TREC RAG datasets, and I've heard from a bunch of people in various industries who got great results by just swapping in the latest Stella model instead of whatever they were using before)

title: Manuel Faysse (@ManuelFaysse)
summary:
Too late to edit my original tweet but super interesting insights from the man, whose twitter handle is not @ "multivector" for a reason. More seriously, I always explain it as "basically simulating cross-attention but at the very end", this goes a lot deeper !
Quoting @lateinteraction
Some quick thoughts: On why we gave the ColBERT paradigm the name "late interaction" instead of "multi-vector", a term that emerged later and that has proven to be more intuitive.
**The mechains is actually not about having multiple vectors at all.** You can see this in four different ways.
1) You can take a ColBERT-like method and try to use a constant number of vectors (e.g., 16) but it will barely outperform having one vector in the general case.
It's not that you need token-level alignment per se (you don't either!) but you want fine-grained representations, not just *multiple* representations.
2) More importantly, there's nothing to say you can't store a TON of information in a single vector. Similarly, it's easy to use multiple vectors and gain *zero* improvement over a single-vector, e.g. if you replace MaxSim with AvgSim in ColBERT, without any other changes, it doesn't work!
The problem isn't the vector representation, it's the **learnability of the scoring function**.
A dot product is just very hard to learn. An intuition I learned from Menon et al (2021) is that: for dot products, every time you "fix" one query--document pair, you likely break so many other pairs by moving the query and/or document representations.
For ColBERT, you typically *fix* more than you break because you're moving *tokens* in a much smaller (and far more composable!) space.
3) "Multi-vector" makes it sound like these approaches win because they store "more stuff".
But that's actually not true: if you look at how aggressively compressed typical ColBERT implementations (like PLAID) are, it's often as small as 20 bytes per vector (that's like 5 floats), which makes a document representation often far smaller than the uncompressed single-vector variants people usually deploy.
4) By default, IR methods that use "multiple vectors" (e.g., cross-encoders) are unscalable. The fascinating thing in late interaction is that it's easy to implement in asymptotically sub-linear ways thank to pruning. THAT is worth a lot.
Anyway, it's no big deal, but the term late interaction > multi-vector, in principle, though multi-vector is a lot more intuitive and sticks.

title: Manuel Faysse (@ManuelFaysse)
summary:
"Just use embeddings," they said.
But they never mentioned you need MULTIPLE vectors to truly capture meaning.
Here's the truth no one tells you about single-vector embeddings:
When you encode "A very nice cat" as a single vector [0.0412, 0.1056, 0.5021, ...], you're LOSING information. It's like squeezing an entire paragraph into one emoji - something's gonna get lost.
Enter multi-vector embeddings - a game-changer for semantic search:
𝗦𝗶𝗻𝗴𝗹𝗲-𝘃𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿:
• One vector represents your entire text
• Fixed dimensionality (e.g., 768 dimensions)
• Similarity calculated by direct comparison (dot product/cosine)
• Quick but loses nuance
𝗠𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶-𝘃𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿:
• Multiple vectors represent different parts of your text
• Each token/word gets its own vector
• Uses "late interaction" to compare individual parts
• Preserves fine-grained meaning
Why this matters: With multi-vector embeddings, your search can match specific parts of documents rather than vague overall similarity. It's like comparing ingredients instead of just the general "taste" of recipes.
This approach (implemented in models like ColBERT, ColPali, or ColQwen) enables more precise searching through "late interaction" - matching individual parts of texts rather than comparing them as whole units.
The visualization explains it all: single-vector embeddings compress everything into one point in vector space, while multi-vector embeddings preserve the unique semantic contribution of each word or phrase.
This was introduced in `v1.29` as a technical preview, and is now generally available in `v1.30`. This means that the feature is considered stable and ready for production use. Worth checking out if you've been frustrated with single-vector limitations.
Learn more:

title: Manuel Faysse (@ManuelFaysse) — thread (15 tweets)
summary: [1/15] 🚨 Context matters for effective retrieval—but most embedding models cannot leverage crucial information outside of the passage they embed. Our new paper "Context Is Gold to Find the Gold Passage" explores how context-aware embeddings can be trained to boost performance! 🧵(1/N) 📷 ──────── [2/15] Traditional embedding models split long documents into chunks, then embed them in isolation. In practice, it's often important to have read the rest of the document to understand what the chunk is about - who is "they" in the example below ? (2/N) 📷 ──────── [3/15] 📊 We introduce the Context-aware Textual Embedding Benchmark to measure (on both toy and practical tasks) how retrieval systems are able to leverage document-wide context to accurately embed and retrieve documents when chunks aren't self-contained. (4/N) 📷 ──────── [4/15] The best we have right now are reformulation approaches using a LLM that reads the entire doc and generates a short summary that is prepended to the passage! When the search corpus size is large, this is prohibitively costly... (3/N) ──────── [5/15] Although standard models struggle, the light at the end of the tunnel comes from Late Chunking, a promising approach by @JinaAI_ in which entire documents are fed to long-context encoders before being chunked a posteriori, enabling information propagation between chunks. (5/N) 📷 ──────── [6/15] 1) Negs from other docs encourage information flow between same document chunks. Entities are resolved and chunks from the same document are mapped closer in latent space. 2) On the other hand, the contrastive term between same-document chunks ensures each chunk retains its specificity, and remains identifiable w.r.t. to its neighbors. (7/N) ──────── [7/15] We find we can improve upon this through a custom training strategy : In-Sequence Negative Training. By sampling negative documents for our contrastive training both from other docs (in-batch), and from the same (late-chunked) document, we enable 2 things: (6/N) 📷 ──────── [8/15] Crucially, we find both in-sequence & in-batch negatives need to be used jointly to get the best possible contextualized embeddings! Performance largely drops without both! (8/N) 📷 ──────── [9/15] Interestingly, Late Interaction (LI) models react quite differently to Late Chunking. Without training, LC doesn't help at all (probably due to the fact features remain very token-level). InSeNT yields large performance boosts, showcasing LI + LC are compatible, but they really need to be trained jointly! (10/N) ──────── [10/15] 📈 Results: Late Chunking (LC) alone yields a 9.0 nDCG@10 improvement on ConTEB. LC + InSeNT achieves an impressive average boost of 23.6 nDCG@10! (9/N) 📷 ──────── [11/15] Finally, we also show models contextualized models are more robust to bad chunking strategies, and scale better w.r.t. corpus size! (1) Better retrievers remain crucial in agentic search settings and just "grepping" is mostly a suboptimal strategy. Semantic embeddings enable getting to the answer faster and more often w.r.t BM25.
(2) Having said that, agentic search is clearly the way forward and unlocks most of the performance (on this type of query). Models have much room to improve, enabled by standard protocols around tool use (MCP) and better native reasoning capabilities.
(3) The end users of retrieval models under this paradigm are not humans anymore but LLM agents. As such, retrievers should be optimized for them (optimize recall rather than precision for instance). Joint optimization is key - the paper suggests training retrievers for specific models; on our end, we did some research on optimizing the LLM agent's query formulation given which retrieval model is used using RL.
(4) A key challenge will lie in how to parallelize these operations. Sequentially, the retrieval operations are only a minor share of the total time, figuring out how to distribute the compute optimally is important I feel.
Once again, a paper focusing on key frontier retrieval problems by the awesome @xueguang_ma & @beirmug which I believe will be an amazing playground for retrieval research!

(thus making the sampling theoretically deterministic), LLM APIs are still not deterministic in practice (see past discussions here, here, or here). title: Manuel Faysse (@ManuelFaysse)
summary:
The "RAG is dead" debate often misses the fact that the 10M context window models that are "burying RAG" are probably just doing some form of RAG over their own context. Very unlikely you get any sort of Needle In a Haystack performance by compressing in a fixed sized memory buffer, and the inference cost of quadratic attention is prohibitive at this length.
So you're still "indexing" by constructing a KV cache (+tricks) during the prefill which you store in a data structure, and "retrieving" relevant context in the form of KV caches to feed the model.
Lots of tricks are possible: "landmark attention" learns a representation of context chunks which are matched to queries with cosine distance (sounds familiar), DeepSeek v3.2 stores a compressed representation of the keys to be quickly matched to queries and construct a top k of KVs to "really" feed to the model. Those are just 2 examples amongst open models, no idea what closed models do but I am quite sure it's a lot closer to "RAG" than most sensationalist twitter ragebaiters account for !

summary:
The trick for image input only models is how to train them efficiently. In ModernVBert, we use a Bert text model and replace the input text embeddings by a vision model. After training, removing the text embedding dict and LM classification head gets you a fully visual model!
Quoting @karpathy
I quite like the new DeepSeek-OCR paper. It's a good OCR model (maybe a bit worse than dots), and yes data collection etc., but anyway it doesn't matter.
The more interesting part for me (esp as a computer vision at heart who is temporarily masquerading as a natural language person) is whether pixels are better inputs to LLMs than text. Whether text tokens are wasteful and just terrible, at the input.
Maybe it makes more sense that all inputs to LLMs should only ever be images. Even if you happen to have pure text input, maybe you'd prefer to render it and then feed that in:
- more information compression (see paper) => shorter context windows, more efficiency
- significantly more general information stream => not just text, but e.g. bold text, colored text, arbitrary images.
- input can now be processed with bidirectional attention easily and as default, not autoregressive attention - a lot more powerful.
- delete the tokenizer (at the input)!! I already ranted about how much I dislike the tokenizer. Tokenizers are ugly, separate, not end-to-end stage. It "imports" all the ugliness of Unicode, byte encodings, it inherits a lot of historical baggage, security/jailbreak risk (e.g. continuation bytes). It makes two characters that look identical to the eye look as two completely different tokens internally in the network. A smiling emoji looks like a weird token, not an... actual smiling face, pixels and all, and all the transfer learning that brings along. The tokenizer must go.
OCR is just one of many useful vision -> text tasks. And text -> text tasks can be made to be vision ->text tasks. Not vice versa.
So many the User message is images, but the decoder (the Assistant response) remains text. It's a lot less obvious how to output pixels realistically... or if you'd want to.
Now I have to also fight the urge to side quest an image-input-only version of nanochat...

title: Manuel Faysse (@ManuelFaysse)
summary:
Unrelated to the main content of this post, but I find it crazy so many people have it as their moral "north star" to try to solve immortality.
A society without death is one without renewal nor urgency. If people continue to have children, populations explode, so likely they wouldn't and we'd only live around people that are a few hundred years old. This hinders creativity and fresh perspectives. I believe we enjoy life and our relationships because they end one day; we HAVE to live because we will die.
Less candidly, death is currently a strong (and imperfect) mechanism for power and wealth redistribution - imagine dictators staying in power for millenia or the quadrillionaires building economic empires over centuries that concentrate all wealth.
My point is not at all that doing science is bad. It's that people have objectives they feel are morally absolutely right - a little nuance goes a long way.
Personally, I would rather die than live forever.
Quoting @togelius
I was at an event on AI for science yesterday, a panel discussion here at NeurIPS. The panelists discussed how they plan to replace humans at all levels in the scientific process. So I stood up and protested that what they are doing is evil. Look around you, I said. The room is filled with researchers of various kinds, most of them young. They are here because they love research and want to contribute to advancing human knowledge. If you take the human out of the loop, meaning that humans no longer have any role in scientific research, you're depriving them of the activity they love and a key source of meaning in their lives. And we all want to do something meaningful. Why, I asked, do you want to take the opportunity to contribute to science away from us?
My question changed the course of the panel, and set the tone for the rest of the discussion. Afterwards, a number of attendees came up to me, either to thank me for putting what they felt into words, or to ask if I really meant what I said. So I thought I would return to the question here.
One of the panelists asked whether I would really prefer the joy of doing science to finding a cure for cancer and enabling immortality. I answered that we will eventually cure cancer and at some point probably be able to choose immortality. Science is already making great progress with humans at the helm. We'll get fusion power and space travel some day as well. Maybe cutting humans out of the loop could speed up this process, but I don't think it would be worth it. I think it is of crucial importance that we humans are in charge of our own progress. Expanding humanity's collective knowledge is, I think, the most meaningful thing we can do. If humans could not usefully contribute to science anymore, this would be a disaster. So, no. I do not think it worth it to find a cure for cancer faster if that means we can never do science again.
Many of those who came up to talk to me last night, those who asked me whether I was being serious or just trolling, thought that the premise was absurd. Of course there would always be room for humans in science. There will always be tasks only humans can do, insight only humans have, and so on. Therefore, we should welcome AI. Research is hard, and we need all the help we can get. I responded that I hoped they were right. That is, I truly hope there will always be parts of the research process which humans will be essential for. But what I was arguing against was not what we might call "weak science automation", where humans stay in the loop in important roles, but "strong science automation", where humans are redundant.
Others thought it was immature to argue about this, because full science automation is not on the horizon. Again, I hope they are right. But I see no harm in discussing it now. And I certainly don't think we need research on science automation to go any further.
Yet others remarked that this was a pointless argument. Science automation is coming whether we want it or not, and we'd better get used to it. The train is coming, and we can get on it or stand in its way. I think that is a remarkably cowardly argument. It is up to us as a society to decide how we use the technology we develop. It's not a train, it's a truck, and we'd better grab the steering wheel.
One of the panelists made a chess analogy, arguing that lots of people play chess even though computers are now much better than humans at chess. So we might engage in science as a kind of hobby, even though the real science is done by computers. We would be playing around far from the frontier, perhaps filling in the blanks that AI systems don't care about. That was, to put it mildly, not a satisfying answer. While I love games, I certainly do not consider game-playing as meaningful as advancing human knowledge. Thanks, but no thanks.
Overall, though, it was striking that most of those I talked to thanked me for raising the point, as I articulated worries that they already had. One of them remarked that if you work on automating science and are not even a little bit worried about the end goal, you are a psychopath. I would add that another possibility is that you don't really believe in what you are doing.
Some might ask why I make this argument about science and not, for example, about visual art, music, or game design. That's because yesterday's event was about AI for science. But I think the same argument applies to all domains of human creative and intellectual expression. Making human intellectual or creative work redundant is something we should avoid when we can, and we should absolutely avoid it if there are no equally meaningful new roles for humans to transition into.
You could further argue that working on cutting humans out of meaningful creative work such as scientific research is incredibly egoistic. You get the intellectual satisfaction of inventing new AI methods, but the next generation don't get a chance to contribute. Why do you want to rob your children (academic and biological) of the chance to engage in the most meaningful activity in the world?
So what do I believe in, given that I am an AI researcher who actively works on the kind of AI methods used for automating science? I believe that AI tools that help us be more productive and creative are great, but that AI tools that replace us are bad. I love science, and I am afraid of a future where we are pushed back into the dark ages because we can no longer contribute to science. Human agency, including in creative processes, is vital and must be safeguarded at almost any cost.
I don't exactly know how to steer AI development and AI usage so that we get new tools but are not replaced. But I know that it is of paramount importance.

title: Manuel Faysse (@ManuelFaysse)
summary: After a few months of doing much AI coding for LLM research at Meta, here are my 2 cents. tl;dr: Efficiency has now become much more about great parallelization than fast sequential execution. I find it super fun but for how long? Setup: By default these past weeks, I was trying at every given time of the day/night/weekend to have as many signal-bearing training runs running on GPUs (the limit being my brain and slurm queues) + multiple Claude Code sessions working in the background on ~mildly useful things / side ideas / moonshots / unit tests. When I worked "actively", I usually just added a main Claude Code + IDE for high prio or critical work that needed more supervision or me coding. I was always waiting on something, so there was this constant guilt when going to lunch/sleep/coffee and no Claude Code was running async to me chilling. My schedule was conditionned on waiting for one more run to finish or for a code edit to be written, to then be able to launch the next one before departing from my laptop. In the short term, the speedup is very clear. The biggest difference for me was not so much speed on my main task, but breadth: it became possible to test out/build/improve tons of things which I would never had prioritized before because I always had more urgent stuff to test out - or that the necessary boilerplate was boring me in advance. Now this runs async for free. Beyond experimental ideas, it is now virtually free to create beautiful figures, or even code your own custom experiment tracker which was never worth it before so the overall quality of the work improves on some axes as a free lunch. I felt my role was more about being an continuous idea generator conditioned by a deep understanding of the experiments: the goal was to be able to as quickly as possible launch follow-ups and iteratively build understanding once results come in and repeat. I feel intuition is even more key as we don't really have N days of coding to reflect upon past iterations, and bottlenecks have shifted away from execution. Personally I love it, the barrier to "hard" things is lowered and creativity is left which is what I feel is the best part of my job. Not sure how long this "phase" will last - contrary to many colleagues, I believe good research ideas + reflecting and reacting to experiments will soon be well within reach of LLMs . It has already stopped being fun for those who just love to code. For me it's the most fun I ever had building things and testing stuff, but for how long before my edge will be elsewhere (if anywhere) ? I am now going back to writing my thesis, wrapping up paper writing and preparing interviews... Not having agents in the background kinda feels weird but I also appreciate the slower pace. Let's see how this all evolves!

clean_title: ViDoRe V3 accepted to ACL 2026 with positive feedback from practitioners
summary:
ViDoRe V3 has been accepted to ACL 2026! Much more relevant however are the many practitioners I met in recent days that praised the benchmark for it's quality and clean signal. It's not easy making a good retrieval benchmark (non-saturated, practical, wide domain coverage) but it helps having done 2 imperfect earlier iterations, understanding what is needed, and having 12k hours of human annotation (thanks @NVIDIAAI ) + 6 months of hard work from notably @MaceQuent1
@antonio_loison @antoine_edy) amongst others.
From a scientific perspective, I believe we converged to a nice recipe that scales but remains challenging by mixing careful taxonomy design (@omrani_bilel), synthetic pre-annotations, and humans in many parts of the loop. This is by no means a cheap project - and going forward, non-trivial benchmarks will probably be more and more expensive. Gone are the days where using a LLM to annotate data creates a sufficient proxy for model improvement (ViDoRe V1).
Some people asked me when ViDoRe V4 would be out. I would assume this should not come from us - we are reaching the limits of data annotation, what we need now are fully real queries and real documents from real users of VDR (and more generally IR) models. This comes with data privacy issues and is tough but I believe it should be the north star - too many datasets in IR are completely toy and optimizing them actually hurts the model.
In all cases, ViDoRe V3 has a lot more to offer than just VDR (agents, RAG, etc) and should have at least a few months of non-saturation ahead of it!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HFZWVTXWIAA116y.jpg
clean_summary:
ViDoRe V3 has been accepted to ACL 2026! Many practitioners I met recently praised the benchmark for its quality and clean signal. Creating a good retrieval benchmark that is non-saturated, practical, and has wide domain coverage is challenging, but prior iterations helped us understand what is needed. We also benefited from 12,000 hours of human annotation, thanks to @NVIDIAAI, and six months of hard work from @MaceQuent1, @antonio_loison, @antoine_edy, and others.

From a scientific perspective, we have developed a recipe that scales while remaining challenging by mixing careful taxonomy design, synthetic pre-annotations, and human input throughout the process. This project is not cheap, and future benchmarks will likely become more expensive. The days of relying solely on LLMs for data annotation to improve models are over.

Some have asked about ViDoRe V4, but we are reaching the limits of data annotation. What we need now are fully real queries and documents from actual users of VDR and IR models, which presents data privacy challenges. However, this should be our guiding principle, as many datasets in IR are too simplistic, and optimizing them can harm model performance. ViDoRe V3 offers much more than just VDR and should have several months of non-saturation ahead.

title: Manuel Faysse (@ManuelFaysse)
clean_title: The importance of scaffolding in search systems
summary:
I feel what these results (@mattjustram) mainly show is NOT that retrievers like BM25 are better than previously thought, NOT that GPT 5.5 is amazing at search orchestration, but rather that scaffolds matter a lot in search (and should be reported).
Pi-serini is one of the first non-trivial search specific efforts to give some proper tooling to LLMs (cached results, well defined tool calls) and smashes the baseline with the same retriever and baseline model. @antoine_chaffin 's results with/without the "get_document" tool also vastly differ: purely scaffolding. CC and Codex are good scaffolds by design and also perform very well at search as shown here (although they are not built specifically for this).
What does this mean:
Biggest low hanging fruits right now in search probably aren't through better embedding models (or even better baseline LLMs) but smart scaffolding paradigms (think RLMs @a1zhang, Pi-serini @lintool, Deep Research systems @din0s_ ).
As LLMs get better, I would expect inductive biases cooked in the scaffolds to become less important than now. However, scaffolds will still need to be expressive enough to let the baseline model "cook" and still need to encode what matters to the end user (speed matters a lot, search is not just accuracy).
Importantly, I believe scaffolds are not an inference time thing only, but should serve during document indexing. To properly contextualize documents in a corpus, we need to move away from the "1 paragraph/webpage is 1 document" concept and use agents to properly map the corpus space, and leverage their priors to index then retrieve. Test time compute scaling is not reserved to querying agents!
Just a few thoughts on recent results, this direction will be well aided by novel datasets like @dianetc_ 's Obliq-Bench which will necessarily require a change in paradigms, the easiest surely being around scaffolding.

📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HILypaZW8AAeSOa.jpg

I feel what these results from @mattjustram mainly show is not that retrievers like BM25 are better than previously thought, nor that GPT 5.5 is amazing at search orchestration, but rather that scaffolds matter a lot in search and should be reported.

Pi-serini is one of the first non-trivial search-specific efforts to provide proper tooling to LLMs (cached results, well-defined tool calls) and significantly improves the baseline with the same retriever and baseline model. @antoine_chaffin's results with and without the 'get_document' tool also differ vastly, highlighting the importance of scaffolding. CC and Codex are good scaffolds by design and perform very well in search, although they are not built specifically for this purpose.

The biggest low-hanging fruits in search right now probably aren't through better embedding models or even better baseline LLMs, but rather through smart scaffolding paradigms (think RLMs @a1zhang, Pi-serini @lintool, Deep Research systems @din0s_). As LLMs improve, I would expect the inductive biases baked into the scaffolds to become less important, but scaffolds will still need to be expressive enough to allow the baseline model to 'cook' and encode what matters to the end user, including speed, as search is not just about accuracy.

Importantly, scaffolds should not only be an inference-time consideration but should also assist during document indexing. To properly contextualize documents in a corpus, we need to move away from the 'one paragraph/webpage is one document' concept and use agents to effectively map the corpus space, leveraging their priors to index and retrieve. Test time compute scaling is not reserved for querying agents!

Just a few thoughts on recent results; this direction will be well aided by novel datasets like @dianetc_'s Obliq-Bench, which will necessitate a change in paradigms, particularly around scaffolding.

title: Manuel Faysse (@ManuelFaysse)
clean_title: Self-Pruned Key-Value Attention: Learning When to Write by Predicting Future Utility
summary:
How do we teach LLMs to learn what they can forget ? A technical break down of the Self-Pruned KV Attention mechanism with fun ML techniques ⤵️
The SP-KV mechanism works by projecting a token's hidden state into a sigmoid to get a scalar "future utility" score for every attention KV pair. At inference, key-value pairs under a certain utility threshold get discarded, freeing up KV cache memory (see the paper thread for details).
Training is a lot more involved! ML experts might recognize that conditionally using a KV pair or not based on the utility value is a non-differentiable if/else where gradient cannot flow. We approach this problem 2 ways:
First, during training, we model the SP-KV mechanism as an attention mask bias. A KV utility value of 0 gets an attention mask bias of -infinity, preventing the key to be used in the attention computation (like the causal mask). A KV utility of 1 gets a bias of 0, enabling full use. Instead of binarizing the utility like at inference, we set the bias to log(utility), enabling us to softly interpolate between the two extremes. This enables full gradient flow: both the signal of "should a KV be more used" and "should a KV be less used" gets preserved. By optimizing NTP, the utility predictor implicitly learns to distinguish KVs that should be memorized from others, and WITHOUT OTHER INCENTIVES, the model learns to use only a fraction of KVs for long range attention. This is basically an extra degree of freedom in attention that improves the loss with respect to standard attention.
Importantly, the utility prediction can choose to open all gates, yielding a mechanism that is equivalent to Vanilla attention. During training, we often start from a normal checkpoint, bias the utility predictor to initialize with all gates open, then let the model self-sparsify and learn to leverage this extra DOF.
Since we still want to threshold at inference to remove low utility KVs, this "soft gating" would create a slight train/test discrepancy. Towards the very end of training, we freeze the utility predictor (detaching the gradient), and binarize the utility value with a given threshold like we would at inference. The mask bias is thus not continuous anymore (either 0 or -inf), which corresponds to the test time regime, which we let the LLM adapt to for a little while. Interestingly, the threshold value we choose at this point enables us to tradeoff performance for sparsity (0.5 is the default, but 0.7 would lead to more forgetting at a slight performance cost).
A fun alternative to soft gating with log(utility) is what we call "hard gating". To reduce test-time discrepancy, we want to train with binary open/close gate decisions (a KV is either used in the attention or not, no in between). To preserve gradient flow, we rely on a Straight-Through Estimator: the forward pass is binarized like at inference, while the backward pass acts as a soft gate with the log scaling.
To preserve the counterfactual gradient of closed gates (what would have happened were this gate were to be open), open or close decisions are made with a Bernoulli sampling of the utility (a KV with predicted utility 0.1 still has a 10% chance of being opened during the forward pass). The combination of Bernoulli sampling and the STE basically simulates soft gating while reducing test-time discrepancies. In the paper, we mostly use soft gating but I thought this was a fun bit of ML to discuss.
The tl;dr here is that SP-KV is just an extra degree of freedom the attention mechanism learns to use to shut down gates in long range attention. It can be learned implicitly and improves the loss, but forcing a binary decision induces a slight test-time discrepancy we need to mitigate!
clean_summary:
This tweet explains a technique called Self-Pruned KV Attention, which helps large language models learn when they can forget certain key-value pairs during attention. The mechanism assigns a utility score to each KV pair using a sigmoid projection, and low-utility pairs are discarded at inference to save memory. During training, the utility score is modeled as an attention mask bias, allowing gradients to flow smoothly through a soft interpolation between using and ignoring KVs. This enables the model to learn which KVs are important for long-range attention, effectively giving the attention mechanism an extra degree of freedom to improve performance.

At the end of training, the utility predictor is frozen and binarized based on a threshold, mimicking the inference process. To reduce discrepancies between training and testing, a hard gating approach uses a Straight-Through Estimator with Bernoulli sampling, allowing the model to learn binary decisions while preserving gradient flow. Overall, this method teaches the model when to keep or forget information, improving efficiency and performance in long-range attention scenarios.

clean_title: Rethinking retrieval research for a transformative LLM moment
summary:
I have a deeper note to make about this: we need to rethink how we approach retrieval research if we want to have an LLM moment.
I think a problem we have as a sub-field is a lack of openness to early research that might be paving the way to what comes next, even if it's not all that good yet.
Let me explain: You might've noticed that we wrote both paper&blog in a way that almost doesn't care that the results are impressively good (essentially sparse SOTA for ~bert-sized model models).
The reason for this is that I truly don't think that the retrieval performance matters here, beyond proving that the method contains signal.
There has been a lot of progress in (applied) retrieval world and embeddings in the last few years, but one thing is still pretty apparent: we understand very little about how things work, and why they work. We've developed better methods, but they are largely a result of more compute + more refined pipelines + more training, etc. It works, but it's brute-forced, and the results are improving but not revolutionising the world.
Between 2020 and now, our understanding of what makes a retrieval model "good" has progressed, but not to the extent that we know what *makes* it work. ColBERT's maxsim operator, perhaps unbeknownst to @lateinteraction at the time, is still one of the most informative tool, because it shows us what's possible when we go beyond expressivity-limited scoring operators, even if it's still incredibly naive.
One thing that I'm very proud of is that at @mixedbreadai, we made a bet that the way representations are expressed almost matters less than how it is used, which has justified a lot of our (very time-consuming) engineering and research decisions, but I think it's the right decision to actually understand how neural representations can lead to better retrieval. We've pushed late interaction pretty far, and we are very much working on the next steps of late interaction, one discovery at a time.
Information retrieval is a family of tools. Single-vector models, multi-vector models, SPLADE, etc... are just some of the tools in our toolkit. Making them iteratively better is not, IMO, how we get to the end goal. Understanding *what* makes a given method better and going all-in on figuring out what its representations can tell us about training and representation dynamics is, I think, the right way forward.
Back to my original point: we need to encourage more out-there, kooky ideas that are currently borderline useless but show great promise towards the future!
One of my problem with some of the formal review cycles is that far too much importance is placed on what, I feel, should be an entirely separate, more engineering-focused paper: does this run in XXms? How does it perform on TREC-DL? What's the index size?
These are valid questions. But they shouldn't be asked of work that is exploring concepts. To me, it feels like rejecting Attention is All You Need because it's pointless to rely on a quadratic method to convey information across tokens, it'll never scale.
I want to read more exploratory work whose limitation is basically "okay yeah, we can't really deploy this, but there is undeniably something going on here. It might take 3 more papers, but we need to understand it. We can make it scale later.". I want more of these to spark discussions at conferences about the why, with the how staying at the conceptual level -- "how" at production-scale can come later.
Honestly, I even want to read papers that aren't quite sure why something works, but that have some informed opinions about it and want to show that it does.
When writing the SAE+BM25 paper, I actually had started a whole section on efficiency, making the model more or less sparse, how it impacts performance and vocab distribution, etc... Then I decided to take it all out: pages are limited, and that's not the message I want the reader to get out of the paper. The message is that these indexable sparse structures emerge from dense models. That's incredibly cool. It opens up the door to dozens of follow-up studies. Maybe it's one of the early signals that will lead to a major breakthrough in a paper or ten.
An efficiency study would be spending time and space on things that are worth studying, but are an entirely orthogonal point that should be made separately.
I have the freedom to do this because I have the incredible luxury of working at a very strongly-minded industry lab. We get daily feedback from users and know what matters and what doesn't, and if the paper gets rejected, it will have absolutely no impact on my work or career. Many, many extremely talented researchers don't have that luxury, and spend precious human and GPU-weeks on optimising for the wrong problems, too early.
And optimising for efficiency before discovering the true performance potential is one of the best ways to miss the big discovery in exchange for a smaller but more guaranteed payoff.
In LLM world, the massive breakthroughs came from similar freedom from worries. Scaling to GPT-2 made absolutely no sense from a publishable unit or GPU-rentability point of view, but it paved the way to understanding the generative potentials of transformers.
I think retrieval is key to the knowledge economy we're going to live in. The smartest agents will need knowledge from the world, no matter how genius they are.
I'm very happy that we're doing this work, but I'd love to see many more people have the ability to join this gigantic effort.
We'd benefit immensely as a field from supporting and celebrating exploratory research that let us develop the new generation of tools that will power this agentic knowledge era.
Quoting @mixedbreadai
By now, everyone knows that single-vector embedding models are hugely limiting for modern workflows.
But they contain than you think: you can extract sparse Latent Terms from them.
And it turns out that BM25 is all you need to turn this vocabulary into a strong retriever.

Faysse advocates for more exploratory, concept-driven research that investigates the underlying representations and dynamics, even if these ideas are not immediately deployable. He stresses that supporting unconventional ideas can lead to fundamental advances, similar to how scaling to GPT-2 unlocked new potentials in generative modeling. summary:
That's why models that optimize for MTEB triggers me as an information retrieval guy. In IR, embeddings should not aim to "represent" the documents, rather to index them such that associative recall mechanisms are triggered with future queries but index != content
Quoting @antoine_chaffin
Despite being insanely cool results by itself, I think this study highlights something much more important for the future direction of IR
The goal has never been to create representations that contains all the information about the original input.
We know for a very long time (e.g, 2023 from @jxmnop that dense - single vector - embeddings contains enough information to reconstruct the input given enough decoding capability.
The BP frames it very nicely: "the role of the embedding model is to convert the information in the documents into a format that can be readily consumed by the efficient scoring mechanism we discussed above"
What we are trying to do, is encoding this information that is _queryable_ in **sublinear time**. You can pre-compute a very large part of the document representations and only do small cross-encoding operations to recover most of the cross-encoder (reranker performance) (@_VictorMorand_ You would still be unable to search among millions of documents unless you have a first stage retriever that look for this information in sublinear time.
To enable this, information retrieval needs to create a structure that allows to traverse our documents pool quickly while finding everything that is relevant for a query. The dense space does that by leveraging spatial proximity and finding elements that are in the same neighborhood. The sparse space does so by leveraging the overlaps of components activated between two elements. Both shares a lot (and I would love to come up with an unified theory about them), but they are intrinsically representing the information in two different ways that enable fast search.
More than ever it is important to question everything we have been doing and what we know and start asking fundamental questions
We should stop asking ourselves "how do I encode all of my information", but "how do I present the information such that I am able to query it quickly and accurately"
ColBERT models lifted some limitations of dense - single vector - models. But so does sparse retrieval, in a different way. Maybe the question is not which one is going to win, but whether we'll find something even better in the way

The web was never meant to be flattened into text.
Yet most web RAG systems start by parsing HTML --- a complex and lossy process.
🔥 Introducing PixelRAG: the first RAG system that retrieves and reads 30M+ web pages as pixels.
Instead of extracting text, PixelRAG retrieves screenshots and lets a VLM read them directly.
PixelRAG not only preserves visual information, but also outperforms text-based RAG on text-only QA benchmarks by +18.1%.
Why?
(1) HTML-to-text conversion often discards layout, structure, tables, and other useful signals.
(2) We continued pretraining a VLM on web page screenshots and turned it into a surprisingly strong visual retriever.
(3) Recent VLMs are remarkably good at understanding web pages, often with better accuracy and token efficiency than text-only pipelines.
Takeaway: HTML parsing may be one of the biggest self-inflicted bottlenecks in web RAG.

First developed by @Nils_Reimers, it is now maintained and extended by @tomaarsen, who does an excellent job integrating relevant trends in the field. The latest release, Sentence Transformers v6.0, adds MultiVectorEncoder, making ColBERT-style late interaction models a first-class model type for training, inference, and interpretation, alongside dense, sparse, and reranker models.
